subject: math

objective.text: Break a fraction into unit fractions with a tape diagram. Write it as an addition sentence.

explanations.title: Fold a strip into unit fractions
explanations.text: A paper strip is 1 whole. Fold it into 3 equal parts. Each part is 1 third. 1 whole is 1 third plus 1 third plus 1 third.

explanations.title: Read a tape diagram
explanations.text: In a tape diagram, the unit fraction tells the size of each equal part. 5 equal parts that make 1 whole are fifths. 2 shaded parts are 2 fifths.

explanations.title: Fractions greater than 1
explanations.text: Some fractions are more than 1 whole. 4 fourths make 1 whole. 4 fourths and 3 fourths more are 1 and 3 fourths.

explanations.title: Number bond and addition sentence
explanations.text: A number bond shows a whole broken into parts. Each part matches one addend in an addition sentence.

examples.title: 1 as thirds
examples.text: The strip is cut into 3 equal parts. 1 equals 1 third plus 1 third plus 1 third. Shade 2 thirds, and 1 third is left.

examples.title: 5 sixths as unit fractions
examples.text: 5 sixths is 5 units of 1 sixth. Add 1 sixth five times to make 5 sixths.

examples.title: 6 fifths on a tape diagram
examples.text: 5 equal parts make 1 whole. One more fifth is after the whole. The tape shows 6 fifths, or 1 and 1 fifth.

hints.text: The strip or tape is 1 whole. Equal parts make up the whole.
Count the equal parts in the whole first.
One part is the whole shared into equal parts. Use division.
The bottom number tells how many equal parts make the whole.
Add the same unit fraction again and again. Keep count of how many.
Picture the strip folded. Count the creases and the parts.
Draw a number bond. Put the whole on top and the unit fractions below.
Think about area. Cut the pieces apart and see if they cover the same space.

misconceptions.label: Equal parts must look alike
misconceptions.description: Child says the diagonal cuts do not make fourths because the triangles do not look alike. Fractional parts need equal area, not the same shape.
detection_signals: Answer says the parts are not fourths because they look different.
Answer says 'they are not the same shape'.
misconceptions.response_text: Parts can look different and still be equal. Fourths need the same area.

misconceptions.label: Mixing up the unit fraction
misconceptions.description: Child names the unit fraction from all the parts drawn, or from the shaded parts, instead of the parts that make 1 whole.
detection_signals: Answer is '1 sixth' when 5 equal parts make 1 whole.
Answer is '2 fifths' when asked for the unit fraction.
misconceptions.response_text: The unit fraction comes from the parts that make 1 whole. Here 5 equal parts make 1 whole, so each part is 1 fifth.

subject: math

objective.text: Break a fraction into smaller fractions with the same unit. Find more than one way.

explanations.title: Number bond for 1
explanations.text: A number bond shows 1 as the whole. The parts are four units of 1 fourth. 4 fourths make 1.

explanations.title: Fold into eighths
explanations.text: Fold a strip into 8 equal parts and shade 7. That is 7 eighths. You can group the 7 units into two parts in many ways.

explanations.title: Same unit in every sentence
explanations.text: All the addition sentences for a fraction add up to the same fraction. The parts all have the same unit, such as eighths.

subject: math

objective.text: Show a fraction as a whole number times a unit fraction. Use a tape diagram.

explanations.title: Multiply instead of add
explanations.text: 3 fourths is 1 fourth added 3 times. When you add the same fraction many times, you can multiply. 3 fourths is 3 times 1 fourth.

explanations.title: Label 1 on the tape
explanations.text: Find 1 whole on the tape first. Count how many units make 1. That tells you the unit fraction. Then count all the units.

explanations.title: Fractions greater than 1
explanations.text: 10 eighths is 8 eighths and 2 more eighths. 8 eighths make 1. So 10 eighths is 1 and 2 eighths.

explanations.title: Sum of two products
explanations.text: 5 thirds is 5 times 1 third. You can also write 1 as 3 times 1 third, and add 2 times 1 third.

examples.title: 3 fourths as a product
examples.text: 3 fourths is 1 fourth plus 1 fourth plus 1 fourth. That is 3 times 1 fourth.

examples.title: 10 eighths as a product
examples.text: 8 equal units make 1. There are 10 units in all. So 10 eighths is 10 times 1 eighth.

examples.title: 5 thirds two ways
examples.text: 5 thirds is 5 times 1 third. It is also 3 times 1 third plus 2 times 1 third.

questions.text: 34 times 22 equals what number?
32 plus 32 plus 32 equals what number?
3 times 32 equals what number?
4 fifths is the sum of unit fractions. How many units of 1 fifth are there?
3 fourths is 1 fourth added 3 times. 3 fourths equals 3 times what fraction?
What is 3 copies of 1 fourth?
1 is cut into 8 equal units on a tape diagram. Then 2 more of the same units are added. What is the unit fraction?
Look at the same tape diagram. 8 units make 1, and 2 more units are added. How many eighths are there in all?
10 eighths is 10 times what fraction?

objective.text: Use an area model to show that two fractions are equal. Write it as a sum and as a product.

explanations.title: Cut each unit into smaller units
explanations.text: Shade 3 fourths. Draw a line to cut each fourth in 2 parts. The whole now has eighths. 6 eighths are shaded.

explanations.title: Sum and product

explanations.title: Double the units
explanations.text: Draw 1 third. Draw 1 line across. The whole has 6 units, not 3. 2 units are selected, not 1. 1 times 2 over 3 times 2 shows this.

explanations.text: Cut 1 half with 3 lines. The whole has 4 times as many units. The selected units are 4 times as many too. Multiply top and bottom by 4.

explanations.text: The units get smaller and there are more of them. The shaded area stays the same. So the fractions are equal.

explanations.title: What happens to the numbers
explanations.text: If you double the number of units in the whole, the denominator doubles. If you double the selected units, the numerator doubles.

examples.text: 3 times 2 is 6, but 4 times 3 is 12. The numbers are not multiplied by the same number. So the sentence is false.

objective.text: Make bigger units from smaller units by dividing. Show that two fractions are equal.

explanations.title: Make groups of units
explanations.text: 6 twelfths has 12 units in the whole. Circle groups of 6 units. There are 2 groups in the whole and 1 group selected. That is 1 half.

explanations.title: Divide the top and bottom
explanations.text: Divide the denominator by the group size: 12 divided by 6 is 2. Divide the numerator by the group size: 6 divided by 6 is 1.

explanations.title: Larger units, fewer units
explanations.text: When you make groups, the units get larger. There are fewer units in the whole. The units are 6 times as large and 6 times fewer.

explanations.title: Pick the right group size
explanations.text: Groups must be all shaded or all not shaded. A factor of both numbers works. For 4 twelfths, groups of 4 work.

examples.title: 6 twelfths is 1 half
examples.text: 12 divided by 6 is 2. 6 divided by 6 is 1. So 6 twelfths equals 1 half.

examples.title: 3 twelfths is 1 fourth

examples.title: 4 twelfths is 1 third

objective.text: Rename a fraction with larger units. Divide the top and bottom numbers by a common factor.

explanations.title: Find a common factor
explanations.text: To make groups, divide the top and bottom by the same number. That number must be a factor of both. 10 twelfths: 2 is a factor of 10 and 12.

explanations.title: List the factors
explanations.text: The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. The factors of 10 are 1, 2, 5 and 10. Both have 1 and 2. Groups of 1 give the same fraction.

explanations.title: A larger factor makes larger units
explanations.text: 8 twelfths: divide by 2 and get sixths. Divide by 4 and get thirds. Thirds are larger than sixths. A larger factor makes larger units.

explanations.title: Use the largest common factor
explanations.text: The largest common factor of 8 and 12 is 4. 8 twelfths is 2 thirds. 2 and 3 share only the factor 1, so you cannot go further.

objective.text: Add and subtract fractions with the same unit. Use a number line and number bonds.

explanations.title: Same unit, same rule
explanations.text: 5 ones minus 4 ones is 1 one. 5 dogs minus 4 dogs is 1 dog. 5 sixths minus 4 sixths is 1 sixth. You subtract the number of units. The unit stays the same.

explanations.title: Subtract on a number line
explanations.text: Mark 5 sixths on a number line. Count back 4 sixths. You land on 1 sixth. For a number more than 1, use a number line from 0 to 2.

explanations.title: Mixed numbers with a number bond
explanations.text: 8 sixths is 6 sixths and 2 sixths. 6 sixths is 1 whole. So 8 sixths is 1 and 2 sixths. This is a mixed number.

explanations.title: Add like units
explanations.text: 1 sixth plus 4 sixths is 5 sixths. 1 one plus 4 ones is 5 ones. You add the units. The unit stays the same.

objective.text: Add and subtract fractions with the same unit, including taking a fraction from 1 whole.

explanations.title: Rename 1 as units
explanations.text: To find 1 minus 3 eighths, the units must match. Rename 1 as 8 eighths. Then 8 eighths minus 3 eighths is 5 eighths.

explanations.title: Count up to find the missing part
explanations.text: Subtraction can be an unknown addend problem. Start at the part you have. Count up to the whole. The jump is the answer.

explanations.title: Subtract from a number between 1 and 2
explanations.text: Break the number into a whole and a fraction. Show the whole as units. Subtract from the total, or take from 1 and add back the extra.

explanations.title: Fraction fact families
explanations.text: Three related fractions make two addition and two subtraction sentences, just like whole number fact families.

subject: math

objective.text: Add two fractions that have related units. Make like units first, using tape diagrams and number lines.

explanations.title: Like units to add
explanations.text: 1 banana plus 1 orange is 2 pieces of fruit. You rename them with the same unit. Fractions are the same. The units must match before you add.

explanations.title: Cut the larger unit
explanations.text: Cut the larger unit into smaller units. You can cut halves into eighths. You cannot cut eighths into halves. Then add the like units.

explanations.title: One denominator is a factor of the other
explanations.text: Thirds and twelfths: 3 is a factor of 12. Cut each third into 4 equal parts to make twelfths. Then add the twelfths.

explanations.title: Estimate, then use a number line
explanations.text: Estimate first. Two fractions each less than 1 half make a sum less than 1. Draw the number line with the larger unit, then cut it into the smaller unit.

explanations.title: Without a model
explanations.text: To add fifths and tenths, multiply the top and bottom of the fifths by 2. Now both are tenths. Then add.

examples.title: 1 third plus 1 sixth
examples.text: 1 third is 2 sixths. 2 sixths plus 1 sixth is 3 sixths. 3 sixths is also 1 half.

examples.title: 1 half in eighths
examples.text: 1 half equals 4 eighths. To add a half and eighths, cut the half into 4 eighths first.

examples.title: Thirds to twelfths
examples.text: Each third is cut into 4 equal parts. There are 4 times as many twelfths in 1 as thirds.

subject: math

objective.text: Add a fraction less than 1 to a whole number, or subtract it from a whole number. Use decomposition and visual models.

explanations.title: Whole number plus a fraction
explanations.text: 2 ones plus 5 eighths is 2 ones and 5 eighths. It is like 2 meters plus 5 centimeters. The two parts are different units, so we write them side by side.

explanations.title: Subtract from a whole number on a tape
explanations.text: Draw the whole number as ones. Cut one of the ones into equal parts. Cross off the parts you take away. Count what is left. The whole number becomes 1 less, plus some parts.

explanations.title: The two fractions make 1
explanations.text: The fraction you take away and the fraction left in the answer are the same unit. Together they make 1. That is why the whole number is 1 less.

explanations.title: Decompose the whole number
explanations.text: To subtract a fraction from 5, rename 1 one as fourths. Draw a number bond: 5 is 4 and 4 fourths. Subtract from the fourths. Then add the ones that are left. It is like unbundling a ten to subtract ones.

examples.title: Fact family with a whole number and fractions
examples.text: Three related numbers give two addition facts and two subtraction facts. One number is the whole. The other two are the parts.

objective.text: Add and multiply unit fractions to build fractions greater than 1 using visual models.

explanations.title: A whole number times a unit fraction
explanations.text: 6 times 1 half means 6 groups of 1 half. You can add 1 half six times. On a number line, that is 6 jumps of 1 half.

explanations.title: Group the halves to make ones
explanations.text: 2 halves make 1. Put parentheses around 2 halves at a time. Each group is 1 whole. 3 groups of 2 halves make 3.

explanations.title: Unit form and the associative property
explanations.text: Write 6 halves as (3 times 2) halves. That is 3 times (2 halves), which is 3 times 1, which is 3. We choose 3 times 2 because we want groups that make ones.

explanations.title: Product as a mixed number
explanations.text: For 9 fourths, count the groups of 4 fourths. 2 groups make 8 fourths. 1 fourth is left. So 9 fourths is 2 and 1 fourth.

subject: math

objective.text: Convert a mixed number to a fraction greater than 1. Use a number line, multiplication, and mental math.

explanations.title: Number bond: ones and a fraction
explanations.text: Use a number bond to split the mixed number into ones and a fraction. Rename the ones as the same unit as the fraction. Then add the units.

explanations.title: Check with a number line
explanations.text: Draw a number line with whole-number endpoints. Mark each whole number in the same unit. Slide from one whole number to the next. Each slide is the same number of units. Add the slides to get the fraction.

explanations.title: Use multiplication
explanations.text: 1 one equals 4 fourths. So 4 ones equals 4 times 4 fourths. Then add the fourths that remain.

explanations.title: Mental math
explanations.text: Picture the mixed number in your head. Think how many ones and how many parts. Find the units in the ones. Then add the extra parts.

subject: math

objective.text: Compare fractions greater than 1 by reasoning with benchmark fractions.

explanations.title: Plot, then compare
explanations.text: Draw a number line with whole-number endpoints. Find the ones in each fraction. Mark the part that is left past the last whole number. The point further right is greater.

explanations.title: Mixed numbers are easier to compare
explanations.text: Rewrite each fraction as a mixed number. Compare the ones first. If the ones are the same, compare the fractions that are left.

explanations.title: A little bit more, a little bit less
explanations.text: A mixed number just over a whole number is a little bit more than that whole number. One just under the next whole number is a little bit less. Use this to compare.

explanations.title: Distance to the next whole number
explanations.text: If two numbers have the same ones, see how far each is from the next whole number. The smaller gap is closer, so it is greater.

subject: math

objective.text: Solve word problems with line plots.

explanations.title: What a line plot is
explanations.text: A line plot is like a number line. We do not put points on the line. We put an X above the line for each piece of data. X's can stack when many pieces of data have the same value.

explanations.title: How to build a line plot
explanations.text: Find the smallest and largest values. Choose endpoints. Pick a unit for the marks that matches the smallest unit in the data. Label the whole numbers. Write the unit below the line, a title above, and a key such as X equals 1 student.

explanations.title: Same units on the line
explanations.text: Some data uses halves, fourths and eighths. Rename them all in the smallest unit, eighths, so you can place each X.

explanations.title: Use the plot to solve
explanations.text: A line plot works like a number line. A value further right is greater. Use the plot to compare, to find a difference, or to count.

subject: math

objective.text: Estimate sums and differences using benchmark numbers.

explanations.title: What is an estimate
explanations.text: To estimate, we do not find the exact answer. We use numbers with about the same value that are easier to work with. The answer is close, but not exact.

explanations.title: Round each mixed number to a benchmark
explanations.text: Think about the nearest whole number or half. A mixed number a little more than 3 rounds down to 3. One a little less than 5 rounds up to 5. Then add or subtract the rounded numbers.

explanations.title: Is the estimate more or less than the answer
explanations.text: If you round up, your estimate is more than the exact answer. If you round down, it is less. Show it on a number line.

explanations.title: A closer estimate
explanations.text: Rounding to the nearest half can be closer than rounding to the nearest whole. Taking a little away from each number keeps the difference about the same.

questions.text: 11 sixths. How many sixths are in 1?

questions.text: You round one mixed number to 3 and the other to 5. What is your estimate for the sum?
You round the same two numbers to 3 and 5. What is your estimate for the difference?

objective.text: Subtract a mixed number from a mixed number.

explanations.title: Count up to subtract
explanations.text: Draw a number line. Start at the smaller mixed number. Add the part that reaches the next whole number. Add whole numbers. Add the last part. The total you added is the difference.

explanations.title: Subtract the ones first
explanations.text: When you subtract mixed numbers, subtract the ones first. Then subtract the fractions from what is left.

explanations.title: Not enough parts: split the fraction you take away
explanations.text: Split the fraction you take away into two parts. Take away one part to reach a whole number. Then take away the other part.

explanations.title: Not enough parts: take out one
explanations.text: After you subtract the ones, take out 1 from the whole number. Subtract the fraction from 1. Add what is left to the rest.

objective.text: Subtract mixed numbers.

explanations.title: Take out 1 from the total
explanations.text: If there are not enough fractional units, rename the total. Take 1 out of the ones. Write it as a fraction. Now you have enough fractional units to subtract.

explanations.title: Subtract the ones, then rename
explanations.text: Subtract the ones first. Then rename the first mixed number by taking out 1. Subtract the fractions. Put the parts together.

explanations.title: The arrow way
explanations.text: Draw arrows to keep track of each step. First subtract the ones. Then count back part of the fraction to reach a whole number. Then count back the rest.

explanations.title: Think of the mixed number as a fraction
explanations.text: You can rename the mixed number as a fraction greater than 1. Then subtract the fractions mentally.

explanations.text: 4 times 3 centimeters is 12 centimeters. The unit stays the same. In the same way, 4 times 3 fifths is 12 fifths.

explanations.text: 4 times (3 fifths) can be written as (4 times 3) fifths. We use the associative property to join the 4 with the 3. The unit, fifths, stays the same.

explanations.text: 3 fifths is 3 times 1 fifth. So 4 times 3 fifths is (4 times 3) times 1 fifth. That is 12 times 1 fifth, or 12 fifths. The unit becomes the denominator.

subject: math

objective.text: Solve multiplicative comparison word problems with fractions.

explanations.title: Three steps to solve
explanations.text: First, model the problem with a drawing. Second, calculate and write a statement. Third, check if the answer is reasonable.

explanations.title: Double tape diagram
explanations.text: Draw one tape for each amount. Make the second tape as many units long as the problem says, such as 4 times as long. Count the units to find sums and differences.

explanations.title: A one-step way
explanations.text: You can find a difference or a total by counting units. If the second tape is 4 times as long, the difference is 3 units. The total is 5 units. Multiply the units by the fraction.

explanations.title: Check each piece
explanations.text: If something is taken from each piece, such as a knot, subtract from both pieces.
